summary: Equal parts of a shape means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into four equal parts as strips, as quadrants, or as four triangles (both diagonals), and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area regions the whole is cut into, and each region is 1/b of the whole. Learners should partition shapes several ways, check equal area by cutting and rearranging or by counting grid squares, contrast valid partitions with unequal 'four-piece' traps, and read a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions rather than cut lines.
misconceptions: Believes equal parts must be the same SHAPE (rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4)
Counts pieces without checking equal area — calls any shape cut into 4 pieces 'quarters', even unequal ones
Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut lines rather than the number of regions
Thinks only the 'standard' partition (e.g. four small squares) is correct

activities.title: Quarter a square two different ways
steps: Take a square and cut (or draw cut lines) to make 4 equal parts.
Now make 4 equal parts a DIFFERENT way — e.g. four vertical strips, then four quadrants, then four triangles using both diagonals.

For each attempt, check that every part covers the same amount: cut and rearrange the parts to see if they match, or draw the square on grid paper and count the squares (putting half squares together) in each part.
Label each part 1/4 and state in words why it is one quarter.
Compare a set of four triangles with a set of four strips: confirm both read 1/4 even though they look nothing alike.
activities.insight: Parts that look completely different can each be 1/4 as long as their AREAS are equal and together they cover the whole.

activities.title: Spot the trap: four pieces vs four equal parts
steps: Look at a square cut into four pieces of clearly different sizes. Decide: is each piece a quarter? Explain.
Check by comparing the areas — on squared/grid paper, or by cutting and rearranging the pieces to see if they match.
State whether 'four pieces' is the same as 'four equal parts', and why.
Sort several partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not': include an equal-area-but-different-shape example (YES) and a four-unequal-pieces example (NO).
activities.insight: Counting four pieces is not enough — a quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters even though there are four of them.

activities.title: Read a pre-partitioned shape: count regions, not lines
steps: Given a shape already cut into equal parts, first check the regions really are equal in area.
Count the number of equal REGIONS (the parts), not the number of cut lines.
Write the unit fraction for one part, e.g. 1/5 for one of five equal regions.
Check your reasoning on a case with three parallel cut lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4 — not 1/3.
activities.insight: The denominator is the number of equal regions the whole is cut into, so you count the parts, not the cuts; and the regions must be equal in area before you name the fraction.

activities.title: Prove two different shapes are equal area
steps: Pick a differently-shaped candidate quarter (a triangle, an L-shape, a strip) and a square.
Use cut-and-rearrange to test whether the candidate covers the same area as a known quarter, or place both on squared/grid paper and count squares, putting any half squares together.
Decide whether the candidate really is 1/4 and justify by area.
Try the diagnostic: show two DIFFERENT ways to split a square into 4 equal parts, label each part, and explain how you know each is 1/4 even when the parts are different shapes.
activities.insight: Equal area can be verified by cutting pieces and reassembling them to fill the other shape, or by measuring on a grid — so you can confirm a differently-shaped part is genuinely 1/4.

checkQuestion: Here is a square. Show me two DIFFERENT ways to split it into 4 equal parts, and label each part. Then tell me: how do you know each part really is 1/4, even when the parts are different shapes?
checkAnswer: Two distinct equal-area partitions (e.g. four vertical strips, and four triangles by both diagonals), each part labelled 1/4. Each part is 1/4 because the four parts have EQUAL AREA and together make the whole — the shape of a part can differ as long as it covers the same amount.
